title: In a simulated Japan Coast Guard trial at the Tokyo Wan Vessel Traffic Service Center, Fujitsu's Zinrai collision-risk predictions help controllers warn vessels about two minutes earlier and nearly double the warnings
summary: In a simulation of past near-miss cases at a Tokyo Bay traffic center, collision-risk predictions from Fujitsu Human Centric AI Zinrai helped controllers send warnings about two minutes earlier.
account: From December 2019 to March 2020, Fujitsu Limited and the Japan Coast Guard tested an artificial-intelligence system to predict vessel collisions at the Tokyo Wan Vessel Traffic Service Center. The center provides navigation support under an outsourcing contract with the Coast Guard. The system uses Fujitsu Human Centric AI Zinrai from Fujitsu Laboratories. The technology detects near misses between vessels and predicts areas where collision risk concentrates in Tokyo Bay. In the center's training environment, six experienced maritime traffic controllers and instructors simulated control tasks based on past near-miss accidents. They compared conventional operation with operation supported by risk information that the system computed from past Automatic Identification System (AIS) data and Coast Guard risk-recommendation records. The risk information shortened the time before a controller sent a risk warning to a vessel by an average of about two minutes. In the simulation, the number of warnings issued to risk-prone vessels nearly doubled. Fujitsu reports that the technology was particularly effective for newcomers. The 2020 results come from a simulation of past cases. Fujitsu announced the figures in a press release of 15 April 2020, and The Maritime Executive restated them the same day. The article cites the Japan Transport Safety Board's count of 2,863 marine collisions in Japan from 2009 to 2019. In the release the Japan Coast Guard said that it would verify more complex traffic conditions and improve the accuracy of the technology as it planned to implement the development. Fujitsu then ran a second field trial at the same center from 17 November 2020 to 2 September 2021 with an added course-following algorithm. Fujitsu reported about 90% fewer unnecessary alerts than with the earlier technology, and it planned a commercial navigation-support service from March 2022.

In the center's training environment, six experienced maritime traffic controllers and instructors simulated control tasks based on past near-miss accidents. They compared conventional operation with operation supported by risk information computed from past AIS data and Coast Guard risk-recommendation records. fields.summary: In a simulation of past near-miss cases at a Tokyo Bay traffic center, collision-risk predictions from Fujitsu Human Centric AI Zinrai helped controllers send warnings about two minutes earlier.
fields.account: From December 2019 to March 2020, Fujitsu Limited and the Japan Coast Guard tested an artificial-intelligence system to predict vessel collisions at the Tokyo Wan Vessel Traffic Service Center. The center provides navigation support under an outsourcing contract with the Coast Guard. The system uses Fujitsu Human Centric AI Zinrai from Fujitsu Laboratories. The technology detects near misses between vessels and predicts areas where collision risk concentrates in Tokyo Bay. In the center's training environment, six experienced maritime traffic controllers and instructors simulated control tasks based on past near-miss accidents. They compared conventional operation with operation supported by risk information that the system computed from past Automatic Identification System (AIS) data and Coast Guard risk-recommendation records. The risk information shortened the time before a controller sent a risk warning to a vessel by an average of about two minutes. In the simulation, the number of warnings issued to risk-prone vessels nearly doubled. Fujitsu reports that the technology was particularly effective for newcomers. The 2020 results come from a simulation of past cases. Fujitsu announced the figures in a press release of 15 April 2020, and The Maritime Executive restated them the same day. The article cites the Japan Transport Safety Board's count of 2,863 marine collisions in Japan from 2009 to 2019. In the release the Japan Coast Guard said that it would verify more complex traffic conditions and improve the accuracy of the technology as it planned to implement the development. Fujitsu then ran a second field trial at the same center from 17 November 2020 to 2 September 2021 with an added course-following algorithm. Fujitsu reported about 90% fewer unnecessary alerts than with the earlier technology, and it planned a commercial navigation-support service from March 2022.
